title: DRP Office Hours and New Data Rescue Workflow
content:
We are excited to announce that over the course of this summer, due in no small part to the hard work of our wonderful metadata analyst and volunteer coordinator, we have overhauled our data rescue workflow! While our data inventory spreadsheet served us well, we are now transitioning to a model centered on sustainability. We are focused on automating workflows to enable easier and faster data rescue. This new process also ensures the rescued datasets are discoverable quicker, so that they can be used more readily by those who need them.

Join us on September 9, 12-1 pm Eastern for an office hour centered on this improved workflow. We will give a demo as well as answer any questions you may have. Additionally, we'll preview some exciting resources coming down the pike for volunteers! Register to receive the Zoom invite. 

https://upenn.zoom.us/meeting/register/yOBHCsoNSiWyHEQmKhKHJw

title: Understanding Federal Data Loss and Future Directions
content:
At just about every presentation, webinar, interview, and hackathon, not to mention in-passing conversations and speculative Bluesky posts, we’re asked: “But exactly how many datasets have been removed since January 2025?”

As we have stated since the start, this is an impossible question to answer for a wide variety of reasons. But a recent report by Christopher Marcum, "The Integrity of Public Access to Federal Data," sheds additional light and nuance on this difficult question.

Some highlights from the report:

  • Approximately 3,000-4,000 datasets have been removed from public access, some of which have been captured by data rescue efforts, while the status of others is unknown. 
  • Importantly, many data tools have been targeted, while the underlying data remain accessible, either in the original location or through rescue platforms. However, these interpretative and filtering tools are what make the data actually accessible to the public. In other words, rather than data loss, the deprecation of analysis tools reduced the utility and interpretability of the data.
    • The loss of EJ Screen is an example of one of those tools.

title: New Report Documents Continued Staffing, Leadership Strains at Federal Statistical Agencies
content:
Below is a guest post from Michelle Crosby and Steve Pierson of the American Statistical Association.

The American Statistical Association (ASA) “FedStat Health” project team recently released its mid-year status report, 2026 Midyear Update: Resources and Leadership Supporting Federal Statistics. As someone who spends every day monitoring, analyzing, and advocating for our nation’s data infrastructure, we are pleased to share key takeaways with the Data Rescue Project community—because the health of our federal statistical agencies directly impacts the data we all rely on. We would also like to request your help.

Federal statistical agencies—from the Bureau of Labor Statistics and the Census Bureau to the National Center for Health Statistics—form the bedrock of evidence-based policymaking, public health monitoring, and socio-economic research. When these agencies face systemic hurdles, federal data more broadly is impacted.

title: Urgent: Oppose NARA Facility Closures
content:
We recently learned that some regional facilities of the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) are being targeted for closures, including the ones in San Francisco/San Bruno, CA and Chicago. These facilities hold important records especially to people in those areas. Among the 100,000 cubic feet of documents in the San Bruno facility -- thousands of which have not been digitized -- there are: 

  • hundreds of thousands of immigration and naturalization materials for people from over eighty countries, including extensive Chinese Exclusion case files -- one of the most comprehensive collections of files connected to the historical immigration through Angel Island; 
  • German, Italian, and Japanese American internment files; 
  • Public Health records; 
  • Mexican Land grant cases; 
  • Hawaiian Birth Certificates and citizenship cases; 
  • and arrival case files for Russian Jews and other immigrants from throughout the world. 

    • Closing these facilities will significantly impede local community access to invaluable materials, including genealogists, educators, researchers, and the general public. We stand by community requests to keep the items as close as possible to where these histories happened.

title: Open for Community Comment: Coalition for Resilient Research Data Infrastructure (CRRDI) Strategic Plan
content:
The DRP Steering Committee is excited about the release of the draft Strategic Plan of the Coalition for Resilient Research Data Infrastructure (CRRDI). DRP Director Lynda Kellam has been working with a committee of experts organized by the Center for Open Science (COS) to develop a strategic plan that promotes and supports resilient infrastructures for federally funded scientific data. This draft plan is the culmination of that effort and is available for community comment. 

The plan is organized around three pillars:

  • Assess and monitor the repository landscape. Building shared, community-led frameworks and tools to understand where the repository ecosystem and the underlying infrastructures are most vulnerable and how those risks change over time.
  • Develop diverse, sustained funding and governance. Coordinating investment more efficiently and building the funding models and structures that let repositories endure.
  • Develop a shared outreach, advocacy, and action strategy. Equipping the community to make the case for sustained investment and to respond when data is at risk.

title: Announcing the DRP Metadata Analyst
content:
Today’s post is an interview with our new Metadata Analyst! The DRP is grateful to be able to offer this position throught the generous support of the Portfolio to Protect Science, a fiscally sponsored initiative of Global Impact, as well as other anonymous individual donors.

We are so excited to have this chance to sit down with our Metadata Analyst! Can you tell us a little about yourself, and what drew you to this position?

Back in 2017, I participated in a data rescue effort through DataRefuge. I distinctly remember being at the JSTOR offices in New York City with a roomful of people rescuing the data in person. Everyone was aware how at risk the datasets were, and there was a great feeling of comradery in the room–librarians, journalists, scientists, data scientists, information activists–learning from one another to rescue the data.

As 2025 approached, it was clear this type of crisis would be happening again.

title: Celebrate Peer Review Week by reviewing together!
content:
To celebrate 2026 Peer Review Week (September 14-18), PREreview is organizing a Review-a-thon: a global event where newly-formed and existing PREreview Clubs synchronously carry out collaborative reviews of preprints and datasets. Our goal is to showcase how human, community-driven peer review can help drive change in the research evaluation culture.

Participating Clubs that organize and carry out at least one collaborative review during Peer Review Week, and publish the resulting PREreview(s)—co-authored by two or more people—within the following two weeks will be entered into a raffle for a 500 USD fund to support further collaborative review activities.

Registration for the Review-a-thon is now open through August 31st. We especially want to encourage participation from communities that review in languages other than English, groups reviewing datasets and data papers, as well as clubs specializing in social sciences and humanities. Gather your lab, classroom, journal club, department, or scholarly community to give constructive feedback on a research output as a team!

title: The Great Federal SOGI Data Rescue
content:
During the Trump administration’s first year, sexual orientation and gender identity (SOGI) measures were widely removed from national surveys, programmatic data, and administrative systems. These changes often happened with little transparency, accountability, or evidence-based decision-making. While the removals have largely impacted data collection and dissemination beginning in 2025, there is a risk that currently available data will be modified to remove SOGI information. Thus, the Williams Institute, ICPSR/DataLumos, Movement Advancement Project, and Data Rescue Project, have joined forces to systematically track and publicly preserve every federal dataset containing SOGI measures.

Since late 2025, the Williams Institute has been documenting the questionnaire text that asked about SOGI in each federal survey, including the year the questions were introduced. During a lively hackathon in May 2026, over 100 attendees from across the country took the following actions to preserve SOGI data:

  • Confirmed whether known SOGI questions were present in current versions of datasets on agency websites

title: Thank you Maggie Levenstein, outgoing ICPSR Director
content:
ICPSR has been an integral partner in the work to back up and advocate for public data. Without ICPSR’s DataLumos, the volunteers of the Data Rescue Project would not have had the infrastructure necessary to make our rescued data accessible. This has been key for the DRP, as our mission has always been to ensure public access to public data can remain a public good - a goal we would not have been able to achieve without the active commitment from ICPSR. Thanks to their support, and the amazing DRP volunteers, we have loaded more than 4,000 datasets since February 2025! 

Our primary supporter at ICPSR has been Maggie Levenstein, who has served as the Director for more than a decade. Although we have been lucky to work with and learn from many ICPSR staff, including John Kubale, Erin Meyer, and many more, Maggie’s support has been unwavering, both in championing DataLumos and advocating for data rescue more broadly. ICPSR recently announced that in August Maggie will be stepping away from the Director position to return to the U-Mich faculty roster and take a well deserved sabbatical in September. We are looking forward to celebrating with Maggie at a virtual celebration on August 11.

content:

title: A Year of Saving Our Signs
content:
The following post is authored by Save Our Signs co-founders Kirsten Delegard, Jenny McBurney, and Amelia Palacios.  

Save Our Signs launched one year ago on July 3, 2025, in response to the Executive Order “Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History” and the related Secretarial Order of the same name. While these orders were vague, we feared that they posed an existential threat to valuable educational materials in National Parks, our nation’s largest outdoor classroom. 

We channeled our concerns into action, inviting people who love the National Parks to create a people’s archive of National Park Service (NPS) interpretive signs. We were amazed and inspired by your response. 

You answered our call with your whole hearts, sending us over 15,000 photographs from every US state and many territories. You combed through old vacation photographs and planned trips to NPS sites to build this community-powered project.

title: DRP Receives "Documents to the People" Award
content:
The DRP Steering Committee is delighted to announce (officially!) that the Data Rescue Project has been selected to receive the 2026 ProQuest/GODORT/ALA "Documents to the People" Award. We are honored to receive this award, and are so grateful to all of the nominators. 

The Government Documents Round Table (GODORT) is a forum for librarians working with government documents who are members of the American Library Association (ALA). We are joining an illustrious group of people and organizations who have received the Documents to the People award, including the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, Free Government Information, and many more. 

This Sunday, June 28th, we will officially receive the award at the GODORT reception. If you’re in Chicago for ALA Annual, let us know! We would love to celebrate with you!

title: Championing Public Data: Recap from IASSIST Keynote
content:
In early June, DRP Director Dr. Lynda Kellam delivered a moving keynote presentation at the annual IASSIST conference. In her presentation, Lynda made the connection between data stewardship roles and civic life. Lynda has kindly made her slides, and a transcript of the presentation, publicly available. But for those who weren’t able to attend, or perhaps just need a mental boost, we wanted to highlight an excerpt:

“In the early days of the Data Rescue Project, journalists would call us the resistance. And I would push back on that framing. In those interviews, I would say our only goal was preservation. I was cautious about the political characterization. At the time, I was protecting my institution, and I understood why that caution was necessary. But I have had time to think about it. And those journalists were right, and I was telling only part of the truth.

title: How the Trump Administration Wants to Whitewash History at the President’s Site
content:
The following post is authored by Molly Blake, co-founder of Save Our Signs and Social Sciences Librarian at the University of Minnesota.

In spring 2025, the Trump administration targeted all National Park Service (NPS) sites with censorship via Executive Order 14253 and Secretarial Order 3431. These orders have resulted in the censorship of dozens of materials from at least 37 different sites. Collectively, these erasures reveal the broad range of empirical statements that the Trump administration wants to suppress from the public: The man who murdered Medgar Evers was a racist. Gustavus Cheyney Doane led the Marias Massacre, which killed over 170 Piegan Blackfeet. Using a water bottle can reduce greenhouse gas emissions. 

Yet these orders name just one NPS site by name: Independence National Historic Park in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.
